title: Commonly Confused Words
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · English: Usage and Word Choice
summary: affect/effect, than/then, its/it's, their/there/they're, principal/principle, complement/compliment, allude/elude, precede/proceed and more — each with a memory trick, worked items and a 10-question ACT-style quiz.

blocks.text: *Affect* or *effect*? *Than* or *then*? *Its* or *it's*? These pairs sound the same (or almost the same) but have different meanings, so spell-check will never catch them. The ACT puts them in essays because a writer who mixes them up looks careless. This lesson groups the most common pairs, gives each one a **memory trick**, and shows how to test the choice in seconds.
What this question type tests

Confused-word questions are part of **Conventions of Standard English** (38–43% of the 40 scored ACT English questions) when the choice is about the correct form, such as *its/it's* or *their/there/they're*, and part of **Knowledge of Language** (18–23%) when the choice is about the precise word, such as *eminent/imminent* or *allude/elude*. The format is the usual ACT English item: an underlined word, four choices, usually **NO CHANGE** first.

A vertical scan of the choices shows two or three words that **look or sound alike**, sometimes with an apostrophe moving around: its / it's / its'. When you see this, ask two questions: **What part of speech does the sentence need here?** and **What does each word mean?**
Group 1: Apostrophe twins (contraction vs possessive)

**The rule that solves all of them:** a word with an apostrophe here is a **contraction** — two words joined. **Expand it.** If the two full words make sense, keep the apostrophe; if not, you need the possessive, which has **no apostrophe**.

rows: **their** = belonging to them · **there** = a place / *there is*
**Who's** coming? The girl **whose** bag is red.

items: ✗ The company changed it's logo. → expand: *changed it is logo* ✗ → ✓ **its** logo.
✗ The museum, who's collection is famous… → *who is collection* ✗ → ✓ **whose** collection.
✗ Their going to win. → *They are going* ✓ → ✓ **They're** going to win.
**its' does not exist.** Any choice with *its'* is wrong.
**Memory trick:** *his, hers, its, theirs, whose* — possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe. If *his* has no apostrophe, neither does *its*.
**their / there:** *their* contains **heir** (a person who inherits — owns something); *there* contains **here** (a place).

blocks.title: افتح الاختصار
blocks.text: لما تشوف it's أو they're أو who's أو you're، فكّها لكلمتين: it is / they are / who is / you are. لو الجملة لسه مظبوطة يبقى الأبوستروف صح. لو مش مظبوطة يبقى عايز الملكية من غير أبوستروف: its / their / whose / your. و its' مالهاش وجود أصلًا.
Group 2: The big four of meaning

rows: affect = verb (to influence) · effect = noun (a result)
The heat **affected** the crops. The heat had an **effect** on the crops.
**RAVEN:** Remember, **A**ffect = **V**erb, **E**ffect = **N**oun. After *a / an / the / any*, you need the noun **effect**.
than = comparison · then = time, next, *in that case*
taller **than** his father · First we ate; **then** we left.
accept = verb (agree to receive) · except = preposition (not including)
She **accepted** the prize. Everyone came **except** Ali.
lose = verb (stop having, fail to win) · loose = adjective (not tight)
*loose* has an extra **o** — it is too loose to hold it

blocks.text: **Advanced affect/effect:** *effect* can also be a **verb** meaning *to bring about*: "The new manager **effected** real change" (= made change happen). *Affect* can be a noun in psychology. The ACT very rarely tests these; if the sentence needs "influence" choose *affect*, if it needs "a result" choose *effect*.
Group 3: Sound-alikes with different meanings

rows: principal = main; head of a school · principle = a rule, belief
The princi**pal** is your **pal**; a princip**le** is a ru**le**.
complement = complete or go well with · compliment = praise
The sauce **complements** the rice. She **complimented** my essay.
allude (to) = mention indirectly · elude = escape, avoid, be hard to understand
He **alluded to** his trip. The answer **eluded** me.
allusion = indirect reference · illusion = false appearance
precede = come before · proceed = go forward, continue
A short film **preceded** the talk. Please **proceed** to gate 4.
elicit = draw out (a response) · illicit = illegal
cite = quote as evidence · site = a place · sight = vision, a view
**cite** a source · a building **site** · a beautiful **sight**
stationary = not moving · stationery = paper, envelopes
council = a group that governs · counsel = advice; to advise
desert = dry land; to abandon · dessert = sweet course
de**ss**ert has two s's — you want **s**econd **s**weets
bad **weather** / I don't know **whether** to go.
passed = verb (went by) · past = earlier time; beyond
The bus **passed** us. in the **past** / walked **past** the shop
If you need a verb, use **passed**.
conscience = moral sense (noun) · conscious = awake, aware (adjective)

blocks.text: Group 4: Look-alikes in meaning (precision)

rows: eminent = famous, respected · imminent = about to happen
imply = suggest (the speaker) · infer = conclude (the listener)
Her tone **implied** doubt; I **inferred** that she disagreed.
adapt = change to fit · adopt = take as your own
Plants **adapt** to drought. The school **adopted** a new policy.
emigrate = leave a country · immigrate = enter a new country
She **emigrated from** Egypt and **immigrated to** Canada.
discreet = careful not to reveal · discrete = separate
lie = rest (no object): lie, lay, lain · lay = put (needs an object): lay, laid, laid
I **lie** down. She **laid** the map on the table.
every day = each day (adverb phrase) · everyday = ordinary (adjective)

blocks.text: **Also always wrong:** *could of / should of / would of* (✓ could **have**), *alot* (✓ **a lot**), *irregardless* (✓ **regardless**).

blocks.title: حيل للحفظ
blocks.text: affect فعل و effect اسم (بعد a أو the يبقى effect). than للمقارنة و then للوقت. principal ممكن يكون مدير المدرسة "صاحبك pal"، و principle قاعدة rule. complement يكمّل، و compliment مدح. precede يعني ييجي قبل (pre)، و proceed يعني يكمّل لقدّام (pro). elude يعني يهرب escape، و allude يلمّح.
Worked examples
Each example is a sentence from an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1 — its / it's.** "Every spring the old sycamore in our courtyard drops **it's** seeds onto the stone path, and by summer tiny trees appear between the cracks."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) its'
C) it is
D) its

blocks.text: **Answer: D.**

items: **D is correct.** The seeds belong to the tree, so we need the possessive **its** (no apostrophe).
**A** expands to *drops it is seeds* — nonsense. **Trap:** the apostrophe looks like a possessive.
**B** *its'* does not exist in English.
**C** is the expanded contraction, still meaningless here.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — affect / effect.** "The new timetable had a surprising **affect** on attendance: absences fell by almost a third."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) effect
C) affection
D) effecting

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** After *a surprising* we need a **noun** meaning *result*: **effect**.
**A** *affect* is the verb. **Trap:** RAVEN — after an article, use the noun.
**C** *affection* means love or warm feeling.
**D** is a verb form and cannot follow *a surprising*.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — precede / proceed.** "Before the match began, the referee asked both captains to **precede** to the centre of the field."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) preceed
C) proceed
D) proceeding

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The captains *go forward* to the centre: **proceed** (pro = forward).
**A** *precede* means *come before something*; it needs an object (A speech preceded the match) and does not mean *go*.
**B** is a misspelling.
**D** is a participle, but after *asked … to* we need the base verb.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — allude / elude.** "For centuries, the exact purpose of the ancient stone circle **alluded** historians, who could only guess why it had been built."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) illuded
C) alluded to
D) eluded

blocks.text: **Answer: D.**

items: **D is correct.** The purpose *escaped* the historians' understanding: **eluded** (e = escape). The second part of the sentence (they could only guess) confirms it.
**A** *allude* means *mention indirectly*; a purpose cannot hint at historians.
**B** is not a word.
**C** adds *to*, which makes the idiom correct for *allude* but the meaning is still wrong. **Trap:** fixing the grammar without fixing the meaning.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5 — complement / compliment.** "The bright blue tiles in the café **compliment** the white walls, making the small room feel open and fresh."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) complement
C) complemented by
D) compliments

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** The tiles *go well with* the walls: **complement** (the word *completes* the look). *Tiles* is plural, so the plural verb form **complement** agrees.
**A** *compliment* means *praise*; tiles cannot praise walls. **Trap:** one letter changes the meaning.
**C** creates a passive phrase that leaves the sentence without a main verb.
**D** has the wrong meaning and a singular verb with the plural subject *tiles*.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The apostrophe trap:** it's / who's / they're / you're for possession — expand the contraction to test it.
**its' and their's:** never correct.
**affect after an article:** a/an/the + *effect* (noun).
**then in a comparison:** better then → better **than**.
**One-letter twins:** lose/loose, quiet/quite, principal/principle, complement/compliment, precede/proceed.
**Fixing grammar but not meaning:** *alluded to historians* is grammatical but still means *hinted at*.
**could of / should of:** always **have**.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Apostrophe in the choices? Expand it. If the full words do not fit, choose the form with no apostrophe.
Ask what part of speech the slot needs: noun (effect, advice), verb (affect, advise, breathe), adjective (loose, conscious).
Say a short definition of each word in your head and put it in the sentence.
Use the context clue in the rest of the sentence ("could only guess" → eluded).
Eliminate any misspelling (preceed, its', alot) at once.
Revise the memory tricks on this page the week before the test.

blocks.text: Practice
Two short ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers. Every question tests commonly confused words.

blocks.title: Commonly Confused Words — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays, 10 questions. Choose the best version of each underlined portion; NO CHANGE keeps the original. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
The Thursday Night Market

Every Thursday evening, a small night market opens in the car park behind our school. Local families bring __there__ [1] own food and crafts to sell, and by eight o'clock the whole area is full of light, music and the smell of grilled corn. Since the first night, the market has kept __it's__ [2] two simple rules: no plastic bags, and every stall must close by eleven.

The market has had a clear __affect__ [3] on the neighbourhood. Shops on the nearby streets report more customers on Thursdays __then__ [4] on any other day of the week, and several new cafés have opened. The organisers __accept__ [5] help from anyone who wants to volunteer, so students from our school often set up the tables and collect the rubbish at the end of the night.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: The food and crafts belong to the families, so the possessive **their** is needed before *own*. *There* (A) is a place; *they're* (B) = they are; *theirs* (D) stands alone and cannot come before a noun.

questions.q: [5] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

questions.p:
A New Kind of Exam Week

When Dr. Hoda Nasser became the __principle__ [6] of our school, she made one change that surprised everyone. Before each exam week, every student had to write a short, kind note to a classmate. Some teachers thought the idea was strange, but the notes soon became popular. One girl in my class received a __complement__ [7] on her handwriting from a boy she barely knew, and she kept the note in her pencil case all year.

The reason for the change __alluded__ [8] most of us until Dr. Nasser explained it at an assembly. Students who feel connected to others, she said, are less likely to __lose__ [9] confidence before a difficult test. When she finished speaking, we were asked to __proceed__ [10] quietly to our classrooms, and for once nobody complained.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: The head of a school is the **principal** (your pal). *Principle* (A) is a rule or belief; *principled* (B) means having strong morals; *principals* (D) is plural after *the … of our school* for one person.

questions.e: She received *praise*, so the word is **compliment**, and after *a* it must be singular. *Complement* (A) means something that completes; *compliments* (B) is plural after *a*; *complimentary* (C) is an adjective.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Expand every contraction: it's = it is, they're = they are, who's = who is, you're = you are. Possessives (its, their, whose, your) have no apostrophe.
RAVEN: affect = verb, effect = noun. than = comparison, then = time.
accept = receive, except = not including; lose = misplace, loose = not tight.
principal = main/pal, principle = rule; complement = complete, compliment = praise; precede = before, proceed = forward; allude = hint, elude = escape.
Check the part of speech and the meaning in context — spelling alone will not save you.
